newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rescuers seek crew of Iraq-bound freighter.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers seek crew of Iraq-bound freighter.

text.p: A South African rescue plane searched a remote square of the south Atlantic Ocean on Friday for the crew of a ship that sank in unexplained circumstances while carrying sugar from Brazil to Iraq.

Airforce spokeswoman Marietta Hopley told Reuters the C-130 Hercules aircraft arrived at the scene 680 nautical miles (1,200 km) west of Cape Town about 1430 GMT, some 15 hours after maritime authorities picked up a distress call.
Asked if the search plane had sighted survivors, she said: "Not yet. They've just arrived."
"Visibility is quite good for a search. The weather is fine," Hopley added. The Hercules crew was due to search an area of about 1,000 square miles as long as light lasted.
First reports said all 28 crew members of the general cargo ship Jahan had abandoned ship after the freighter began taking on water, and were presumed to be in lifeboats.
There was no immediate indication of what caused the sinking of the 15,022 deadweight tonne Jahan, built in 1972, registered in Belize and operated by Seatimes shipping of Singapore.
Weather at the time in the vicinity -- a spot in the South Atlantic midway between the South African coast and the remote island of Tristan da Cunha-- was reported fine.
A mayday call picked up by the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Australia around midnight GMT said the freighter was flooding and the crew were abandoning ship.
The centre said the Jahan went down five hours afterwards.
The South African airforce Hercules transport was carrying survival gear, and three ships at sea were also steaming towards the Jahan's last reported position.

Rescue officials said the ships would take several hours to reach the spot, 32 degrees South by 00.45 East. If the Hercules sighted survivors, it would plot their drift rate and relay it to the ships, a Greek crude carrier and two bulk carriers.
Survival gear would be air-dropped if required, the airforce said.
Although there were no reports of injury to the crew, one rescue official said it was unusual that no emergency positioning radio beacon signal was being picked up.

A spokesman for Seatimes in Singapore told Reuters the 8,757 gross tonne motor vessel Jahan, owned by Jahan shipping of Panama, was on charter to a London company and carrying a cargo of 14,000 tonnes of sugar from Brazil to Iraq.

A recent accord between Iraq and the United Nations, concluded after months of wrangling over terms, allows Iraq to sell a certain amount of oil twice a year to pay for food imports, alleviating the effect of U.N. economic sanctions on the Iraqi people.
It was not clear, however, whether the Jahan's cargo was part of the oil-for-food deal.
